newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs support anti-Milosevic protests.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs support anti-Milosevic protests.

text.p: Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic on Tuesday backed opposition street protests in neighbouring Serbia that have shaken the Belgrade government.
Plavsic said the participation of university students in this month's demonstrations revealed the country was facing a political crisis.
"The entry of students always means that freedom and democracy are endangered," Plavsic said in an interview on official Bosnian Serb television.
More than three weeks of protests from the opposition have failed to force Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to accept its victories in annulled local elections.

Plavsic and the rest of the Bosnian Serb leadership have had hostile relations with Milosevic for some time, often portraying themselves as "capitalists" and royalists opposed to the ruling socialists in Belgrade.
The hardline Serb nationalists in Bosnia relied on Serbia as their patron during the war but fell out with Milosevic over his willingness to enter peace talks as the conflict dragged on.
"I was asked how I would react if I was in Belgrade and I said openly I would be there where my students were," said Plavsic, a former biology professor.
"I should like Serbia during these tumultous days to emerge at the end as a strong national country like all European states," she said.

She disagreed with the international preception of Milosevic as a guarantor for the Dayton peace agreement, saying the success of the accords mainly depended on the people and the leaders which it directly affected.
Referring to 50 years of socialist rule in Serbia, Plavsic said "ideological barriers" had cost the Serb people dearly.
She said there was no reason why Serbia had to remain a socialist "enclave" in Europe and that other nations in former Yugoslavia had already rid themselves of the communist legacy.
"Croats resolved this problem very quickly," she said in a reference to Croatia's rapid moves to align its self with Western Europe.
Western countries have expressed sympathy for the street protests that have run for more than three weeks and backed demands for Milosevic to recognise an opposition victory in local elections.
But diplomats are wary of some of the opposition politicians who have publicly supported the hardline Bosnian Serb leadership, including wartime president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.
Milosevic, widely blamed for helping ignite four years of war in former Yugoslavia, has adopted an image as a "peacemaker" and purged prominent nationalists from his ranks.
